tracks.label: Opening
tracks.text: Chapter 2. Core Loops and Mechanics. On 21 December 2023, a 13-year-old in Oklahoma named Willis Gibson did something no human player had managed in the 34 years since Nintendo released Tetris for its home console: he played until the game itself broke. At level 157 the screen froze, and the only opponent left was the code. Gibson had not found a secret ending, because there is none. He had repeated one short cycle of actions (watch a piece fall, slide it, turn it, drop it into place) thousands of times, faster and more accurately than anyone before him. That cycle has barely changed since Alexey Pajitnov wrote the first version in Moscow in 1984, on a computer that could display only text characters. A loop of a few actions has held players for four decades, and this chapter is about how such loops are built. Chapter 1 described a game as a system of rules (mechanics) that produces behavior in play (dynamics) and, through it, experience (aesthetics). This chapter zooms in on the mechanics the player touches directly. Section 2.1 names a game’s verbs and its core mechanic. Section 2.2 shows how actions form loops at three time scales, from a single turn to months of play. Section 2.3 turns to game feel: why the same rules can feel crisp or sluggish, and what research says about juice. Section 2.4 explains emergence, the way a few simple rules can combine into play nobody wrote down. Throughout, Tetris (1984), Super Mario Bros. (1985) and Slay the Spire (2019) supply the examples, and the chapter ends with the first real design step on your pocket card game: defining its core loop.

tracks.label: 2.1 Verbs and core mechanics
tracks.text: Section 2 point 1. Verbs and core mechanics. Chapter 1 split a game into mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics, and argued that designers work from the mechanics outward. This section looks at mechanics from the player’s seat. Whatever the rulebook or the code says, the player meets the rules as a short list of things they can do. Designers call these the game’s verbs. In Tetris you can move a piece left or right, rotate it and make it fall faster. In Super Mario Bros. you can walk, run and jump. In Slay the Spire you can play a card, end your turn, choose a path on the map and choose a reward. Each list is short. A good first test of any design, including your own, is whether its verbs fit on a sticky note. Two definitions are worth carrying around. Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman define a core mechanic as “the essential play activity players perform again and again in a game”. Miguel Sicart offers a more exact version: game mechanics are “methods invoked by agents for interacting with the game world”. His wording does two jobs. It says mechanics belong to agents, so an enemy that patrols a ledge has mechanics too. And his paper goes on to sort mechanics into tiers: core mechanics are the ones agents use repeatedly to reach the state the game rewards; primary mechanics are those a player can apply directly to beat a challenge; secondary mechanics make the goal easier without being necessary. In Super Mario Bros., jumping is primary. Throwing fireballs, possible only after you collect a Fire Flower, is secondary. A verb on its own is cheap. What makes it a mechanic worth designing is what it acts on and what changes afterward. Tetris has three verbs, but they act on seven different pieces, the tetrominoes, in a well 10 cells wide and 20 tall, and every placement changes the board the next piece will fall into. Leave a hole and you have made a problem for your future self. Keep one column open and you are setting up a tetris, four lines cleared at once, the move the game rewards most. The decision is never just whether to rotate. It is what board you want three pieces from now. Ernest Adams and Joris Dormans make the same point about whole games: rules matter less one by one than as a system in which each action changes the state the next action works on. Good verbs often do several jobs at once. Mario’s jump lifts him upward, but in World 1-1 the same button press also stomps a Goomba, bumps a question-mark block to release a coin or a mushroom, carries him over pipes and gaps and, at the end, onto the flagpole. One verb meets many objects, and each object answers it differently. Compare a game that gives the player a separate button for every task: more verbs, but fewer interesting combinations. When designers praise a game’s core mechanic, they usually mean this economy. A few verbs, each useful in many situations, mean that the skill a player builds with them keeps paying off. To find a game’s verbs, start with the inputs and translate them into intentions. A controller has buttons; a player has goals. In Tetris the inputs are a direction pad and two rotation buttons, and the verbs are slide, rotate and drop. In Slay the Spire nearly every input is a mouse click, yet the verbs are richer: attack, block, weaken an enemy, draw, spend energy, skip a reward. Card games are built largely from verbs that move cards between zones: draw (deck to hand), play (hand to table), discard (hand to discard pile), trade, steal, reveal. Your pocket card game from Chapter 1 already has verbs, even if you have not named them yet. The challenge at the end of this chapter asks you to write them down. A common misconception: A game’s core mechanic is its theme, like space exploration or running a farm. In fact, The theme is what the game is about; the core mechanic is what the player repeatedly does. Two farming games can have entirely different core mechanics (one about planting on a timer, one about trading cards), and Tetris has a strong core mechanic with no theme at all.

tracks.label: 2.2 Core, meta and session loops
tracks.text: Section 2 point 2. Core, meta and session loops. A verb becomes a loop when its result feeds the next decision. The core loop is the shortest cycle a player repeats: read the situation, act, see the result, read the new situation. In Tetris that cycle lasts as long as one piece, and Figure 2.1 traces it: a piece appears, the player picks a spot, slides and rotates, the piece locks, rows may clear, and the next piece appears. The researcher Emmanuel Guardiola argues that a list of a game’s actions misses this movement. His model of the gameplay loop describes play as the player passing again and again through states of activity inside the game system, which is closer to what designers actually shape. Loops nest inside one another at different time scales. Studios commonly name three, though the terms come from practice rather than from a fixed standard, so expect other labels in other books. The core loop runs in seconds. The session loop is one sitting’s worth of play with a natural start and end: one game of Tetris from the first piece to topping out, one run in Slay the Spire, one evening’s attempt at Super Mario Bros. on a stock of lives. The meta loop runs across sessions. It covers whatever carries over from one sitting to the next and changes what the next session offers, such as new characters, a larger pool of cards or a harder difficulty setting. A useful test is to ask what the player keeps when they stop playing. Slay the Spire shows all three clearly (Figure 2.2). The core loop is one turn of combat: you draw five cards, read the icons above each enemy that show what it intends to do next, spend your three energy on cards, and end your turn so the enemies act. Around it runs the session loop of a run. You pick a route up the map, enter a room (a fight, an event, a shop or a rest site) and take a reward, often a choice of one card from three, plus gold and sometimes a relic. Your deck changes, so the next fight plays differently. Outside that sits the meta loop. Your score from each run adds new cards and relics to the pool for later runs, and beating the third act with a character opens Ascension, 20 levels that each add a new handicap. The point of nesting is that each outer loop changes the inputs of the loop inside it. A card picked in the session loop changes which hands you draw in the core loop; a card added to the pool in the meta loop changes which rewards appear in the session loop. Adams and Dormans describe this kind of structure as feedback: the output of one part of a system returns as input to another, and the shape of that return decides whether play accelerates, settles or spirals. Tetris has a feedback loop of its own, drawn in purple in Figure 2.1. In a game started at level 0, every 10 lines raises the level, and pieces fall faster as the level climbs, so success in the core loop makes the core loop harder. Chapter 3 studies loops like this in detail. Not every game needs all three loops. The NES Tetris of 1989 has almost no meta loop: nothing you do in one game changes the rules of the next, and the only thing that carries over is a score to beat. People still compete at it decades later. The reverse rarely works. Players spend most of their time inside the core loop, so a meta loop of rewards and progress bars seldom rescues a core loop that is dull to repeat. That is why designers prototype the core loop first, often on paper, and play it many times before building anything around it. When you add an outer loop, ask what it gives the player: a reason to come back, a new decision, or only a number that goes up. A common misconception: A strong meta loop, with daily rewards, levels and collectible extras, is what makes a game good. In fact, Meta loops give players reasons to return, but players spend most of their time in the core loop. NES Tetris has almost no meta loop and is still played competitively; a weak core loop wrapped in rewards tends to feel like a chore.

tracks.label: 2.3 Game feel and juice
tracks.text: Section 2 point 3. Game feel and juice. Two games can share the same rules and still feel completely different in the hands. Steve Swink’s book Game Feel gave designers a vocabulary for that difference. He defines game feel as “real-time control of virtual objects in a simulated space, with interactions emphasized by polish”. Each part of the definition does work. Real-time control means the player steers continuously and the game answers fast enough that intention, action and response feel like one unbroken loop. Simulated space means there is a world with movement and collision for the controlled object to act in. Polish means the animation, effects and sound that sell an interaction without changing the simulation underneath. The definition is deliberately narrow: by requiring real-time control, it leaves out turn-based games such as chess and Slay the Spire. Swink breaks feel into parts a designer can adjust: input (the physical device), response (how the game turns input into motion), context (the spaces and obstacles that give motion meaning), polish, metaphor (what the object is meant to be) and rules. On response, he draws on research about human perception to argue that the game must answer within roughly a tenth of a second for control to feel immediate. Mario’s jump, which Swink analyzes in detail, is a model of response design. Hold the button longer and Mario jumps higher; build speed by running and the same jump carries farther. The player is not choosing among a few fixed jumps but shaping each one, which is how a single verb can carry a whole game. Feel also comes from timing rules most players never see. In NES Tetris, holding left or right moves the piece one column at once, then waits 16 frames (about a quarter of a second at the console’s 60 frames per second) before repeating, and then moves one column every 6 frames, roughly 10 columns a second. This delayed auto shift stops a brief press from sending a piece too far, so slow play feels precise. But gravity rises with the level. At level 0 a piece falls one row every 48 frames; from level 19 it falls a row every 2 frames, and at level 29 a row every frame. At that speed a held direction cannot carry a piece across the well before it lands, so for decades players called level 29 the kill screen. Juice is the informal name for polish turned up high: screen shake when something lands, particles when a block breaks, a sound and a flash for every hit. Researchers have tried to pin the idea down and test it. Kieran Hicks and colleagues asked game developers what makes feedback juicy and built a framework for analyzing it from their answers. Experiments suggest juice helps, up to a point. Jesper Juul and Jason Begy built two versions of one game that played identically, one with minimal feedback and one with heavy, redundant sound and animation; players preferred the juicy version, but it did not make them play better. Dominic Kao built four versions of an action role-playing game, with no, medium, high and extreme juiciness. Medium and high levels beat both none and extreme on player experience, motivation, play time and performance. Two practical lessons follow. First, feel lives mostly in the core loop, because that is where the player’s hands spend their time, so tune response and context before anything else. Second, juice amplifies a loop that already works but cannot fix one that does not, and too much of it gets in the way, as Kao’s extreme condition showed. A quick test is to switch the effects off: if the game is still worth playing, the polish is adding to it; if not, the problem lies deeper. Paper games have feel too. The slap of a card on the table in a speed game, the riffle of a shuffle and the click of chips are input and response in the physical world, and you can design your pocket card game around them. A common misconception: Game feel is about graphics, and adding more effects always makes a game feel better. In fact, Most of game feel comes from response and context: how quickly and how expressively the game answers input, and what the space asks of the player. Effects help only up to a point; in Kao’s study, extreme juiciness did worse than moderate amounts.

tracks.label: 2.4 Emergence
tracks.text: Section 2 point 4. Emergence. Emergence is what happens when simple rules, interacting, produce patterns that no single rule describes; Salen and Zimmerman treat it as one of the defining properties of games as systems. The cleanest demonstration is not a commercial game. In October 1970, Martin Gardner’s “Mathematical Games” column in Scientific American introduced a solitaire game invented by the mathematician John Conway, called Life. The board is a grid of cells, each alive or dead. Each generation, a dead cell with exactly three live neighbors comes alive, a live cell with two or three live neighbors survives, and every other live cell dies. That is the whole rulebook. Yet a five-cell shape called the glider crawls across the grid, rebuilding itself one cell over every four generations (Figure 2.3). No rule mentions movement. Board games have shown emergence for centuries. The rules of chess fit on a page, yet in 1950 Claude Shannon estimated the number of possible chess games at around 10¹²⁰, far more than could ever be played. From those rules came a body of knowledge the rules never mention: named openings, pawn structures, the advice that a knight on the edge of the board is weak. Players discovered all of it. Jesper Juul calls such games games of emergence, in which a few rules combine into large variation, and contrasts them with games of progression, in which the designer lays out a series of challenges with planned solutions, as in a classic adventure game. Most games, he argues, mix the two. Our running examples sit at different points on Juul’s scale. World 1-1 of Super Mario Bros. leans toward progression: the designers placed every Goomba and block, and Chapter 6 reads it as a planned lesson. Tetris leans toward emergence: seven shapes and a few rules produce a different board every game. Slay the Spire does both. Its acts and bosses form a progression, but its cards and relics combine in ways no one listed in advance. The card Corruption makes Skills cost nothing but exhausts each one as it is played; the relic Dead Branch adds a random card to your hand whenever a card is exhausted. Together they turn every free Skill into a fresh card, a combination players often name among the strongest in the game. The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild (2017) built a whole open world on this idea. At the 2017 Game Developers Conference, director Hidemaro Fujibayashi, technical director Takuhiro Dohta and art director Satoru Takizawa described how the team began with a simple top-down prototype in the style of the original 1986 Legend of Zelda, in which tools combined, such as an arrow shot through a fire becoming a fire arrow. The finished game rests on general rules about elements and the states of objects, which the team called a chemistry engine, so that effects multiply as rules meet. You can see the result in ordinary play. Fire spreads through dry grass and its rising heat lifts a paraglider; a leaf’s gust can push a raft. The designers wrote rules, not solutions. Emergence also happens between the rules and the players’ bodies. The delayed auto shift described in section 2.3 limits a held direction to about 10 columns a second, but every fresh press moves the piece at once. So players learned to press faster than the auto-shift. Thor Aackerlund is credited as the first to master this fast tapping, now called hypertapping. In 2020 a player known as Cheez popularized rolling, in which the fingers drum on the back of the controller and push it against a thumb resting on the direction pad, producing several presses per motion. With these techniques players passed level 29, and in December 2023 Gibson reached the crash at level 157. Emergence gives a game depth no one planned, but the same process yields exploits and dominant strategies, the subjects of Chapters 3 and 4. Playtesting is the only reliable way to find either. A common misconception: Emergent gameplay just means random gameplay. In fact, Life and chess contain no randomness at all, yet both are classic examples of emergence. Emergence comes from rules interacting with each other and with players’ choices; randomness, like the piece order in Tetris, adds variety but does not create emergence by itself.
